questions.prompt: Sami says: "My grandfather used to fish at dawn every Sunday." What does the sentence tell you about the fishing?

options.text: It was a habit he has now stopped.
It happened only once in the past.
He has just started fishing at dawn.
He still fishes every Sunday at dawn.

questions.explanation: "Used to" + base form says two things at once: the action came back again and again, and it comes back no longer — so the fishing was a habit that has now stopped. A single finished action would be told with the past simple, He fished at dawn last Sunday, and a habit that is still alive takes the present simple, He fishes every Sunday.

questions.prompt: Complete: "When we were children, we ___ to my grandmother's village every August."

options.text: used to went
used to going
used to go
use to go

questions.explanation: "Used to" is always followed by the base form of the verb, which gives "we used to go". "used to went" puts a past form and "used to going" an -ing form where the base form belongs, and "use to go" drops the -d, a spelling that is only correct after the helper did, as in "We didn't use to go".

questions.prompt: A survey ranks the picnic 6th among children and 2nd among adults. Which sentence describes that correctly?

options.text: The picnic drops four places among adults.
The picnic climbs four places among adults.
The picnic comes first among adults.
The picnic is equally popular with both groups.

questions.explanation: The picnic moves from sixth position to second, and a move towards 1 is a rise, so it climbs four places among adults. "Drops" describes the opposite move, towards the bigger figures; "comes first" is kept for position 1, which no figure here gives the picnic; and the picnic cannot be equally popular with both groups, since the two columns give it two different positions — equal popularity shows as one shared position, the case the mark "=" signals.

questions.prompt: Your pen friend writes: "Our holiday was enjoyable but rather lazy — we hardly left the terrace." Which activity belongs to a lazy holiday?

options.text: canoeing down a river
a long walk in the mountains
horse riding at sunrise
watching TV all evening

questions.explanation: A lazy holiday asks nothing of your body, so watching TV all evening belongs in that column, next to sunbathing and sleeping late. Canoeing, walking in the mountains and horse riding are sporting activities and fill the active column instead. Note that "lazy" judges the holiday, not the person: an enjoyable holiday can be a very lazy one.

questions.prompt: A tourist finds a short text in her hotel room that opens with "GOOD EVENING, EVERYONE" and contains the words "the voucher enclosed with this letter". Was the message spoken or written, and what proves it?

options.text: Written — only paper can be enclosed with a letter.
Written — the heading is in capital letters.
Spoken — "GOOD EVENING, EVERYONE" is how a guide opens a talk to tourists.
Spoken — the message addresses a whole group of people.

questions.explanation: The opening does sound like a speech, but nothing can be enclosed with a letter except a written document, so that one phrase settles the channel: the message is written. Capital letters prove nothing — they only make a heading stand out — and addressing a whole group is just as normal in a printed notice as in a talk.

questions.prompt: Which sentence uses "would" correctly for a habit in the past?

options.text: As a child I would know all my neighbours.
In those years my father would be a fisherman.
In August my father would drive us to the beach.
Last Friday my father would drive us to the beach.

questions.explanation: "Would" + base form works only for an action repeated in the past, and driving the family to the beach every August is exactly that. Knowing your neighbours and being a fisherman are states, not repeated actions, and a state accepts "used to" alone: My father used to be a fisherman. A single occasion introduced by "Last Friday" needs the past simple: my father drove us to the beach.
